t: Here’s the Thing: We Could Do Something Else
q: There is something deeply injurious to the human spirit about finding ourselves in spots bereft of meaning and agency. You and I were made to matter — and to choose. Viktor Frankl discovered this in a Nazi concentration camp; meaning and agency, he writes, can be found even amidst the harshest brutality.
But the reality of our agency is as durable as ever. It's just become extra good at hiding.
But here it is. The truth is this: you and I could do something else. We could do something besides teaching, besides education. And in doing that, we could still hold our heads high.

But look, the work ahead is going to take whole-souled engagement: intellectually, physically, emotionally, socially, volitionally. In order to fully restore ourselves for such work, I think we each need to grapple with the reality that we don't have to do it.
I think work is kind of like that too — maybe P = wc², in which the (p)otential meaning and impact of a career is equivalent to the (w)ork the career entails times the speed of light squared.
So, look. I'm a person who has spent the last eight years writing blog posts in my spare time for a single driving purpose: I want you to stay in education.

Because for the work to come, we all need to be here because we've chosen to be. Because teaching, fundamentally, is always that: a choice. That's what it was in my classroom today, and that's what it was in yours.
x: He roots the argument in Viktor Frankl's concentration-camp-forged insight that meaning and agency are essential to enduring hardship, applying it to pandemic-era teachers who felt they'd lost control of their work.
The article's central, deliberately risky claim is that teachers could do something else and still hold their heads high -- other careers carry real dignity and impact too.
Stuart's most load-bearing (and self-described 'risky') claim: teachers are qualified to do other meaningful work, and choosing to leave education doesn't diminish a person's dignity or impact.

q: Each instruction should have the clear aim of getting students to do one important thing, and nothing else, at a time. If they are reading their notes, that is all I expect them to do at that time.

In fact, the purpose of silent, independent work on a simple list of questions is to remove any extraneous cognitive load that can distract student attention. As Peps Mccrea writes in his brilliant book Motivated Teaching, motivation is a system of allocating attention. We want students to allocate their attention to their learning and nothing else.

The more a routine is run consistently, the more students are likely to follow a set of instructions and complete a task. Once again, this has the impact of reducing extraneous load as students focus on the task and not on how or why it needs to be completed.
Students don’t need to be moving around or continually writing to be active participants. If every student is actively thinking about a lesson, they are actively participating as well.

For some students, being called on with no prior warning can result in a lot of anxiety. For these students, I walk around the room as they answer written questions or have discussions during a Think-Pair-Share task. I let these students know in advance if I will be asking them to share their answers.
x: One instruction, one task at a time: clear single-purpose directions and silent independent recall remove extraneous load.
The thread connecting them is reducing extraneous cognitive load so attention goes to learning.
One instruction, one task at a time: clear single-purpose directions and silent independent recall remove extraneous load.
Active participation means every student could be called on at any moment, via cold call, no opt-out and simultaneous whiteboard responses.
Anxious students can be protected by warning them in advance when they will be asked to share, without removing accountability.

t: How To Have Behavior-Changing Influence With Students with-students/
q: The Law of Reciprocity says that when you go out of your way to please someone, they’ll want to please you right back. It’s a deep-seated psychological urge that is nearly impossible to resist.
Make your gesture with no strings attached. It’s so simple, yet so powerful. This alone can do wonders.
If you can be consistently pleasant throughout every school day, you have the keys to the kingdom. Rapport will come effortlessly because students will come to you instead of the other way around.
You must, must, must do what you say you’ll do. Few teachers fall into this special category. But if you do, if you can be a person of your word, truly, it changes everything.

You must enforce consequences consistently and be pleasant at the same time . Once you’re able to do this by course of habit, you’ll experience a level of power and leverage over classroom behavior you never thought possible.
You can’t just try it out for a day or two. You can’t fall on and off the horse. The power grows stronger with time and the longer you maintain your new persona.

t: The Power And Pitfalls Of Letting Students Learn Through Experience
q: Having a clear explanation or “worked example” can ease the cognitive burden. And engaging in projects or simulations can add to it in ways that impede learning.

Also, students are most likely to remember whatever they spend the most time thinking about. If they’re learning about the Middle Ages by making a detailed model of a castle, they’ll probably remember more about the process of constructing the castle—figuring out what materials to use, making them fit together—than anything about the Middle Ages.

That’s not to say that kids should just get lectures. Teachers also need to check frequently to make sure students understand the material. They need to ask questions or assign activities that require practice and analysis. But the basic idea is that the teacher should be directing rather than merely facilitating learning.

That mindset is surely one reason teachers are drawn to activities that are largely student-directed and active. But they probably also sense that—as Ashman’s title says about explicit teaching—experiential learning can be powerful. In fact, sometimes it’s too powerful.

There are ways to make simulations work, but they require careful thought and planning. Before students undertake a simulation, they need to have adequate knowledge of the topic—ideally built through explicit instruction.
One study of simulations in social studies classes—titled “Try Not to Giggle if You Can Help It”—found that 12 of 14 had significant problems.
I remember concepts like villeinage and strip-farming from my sixth-grade study of Medieval England, but it’s not because I wiped my hands on the dog. I’m sure my teacher explained them to me.
x: Projects and simulations add to cognitive load and direct attention to procedure rather than content.
Natalie Wexler starts from a vivid memory of a sixth-grade medieval England simulation to ask when experiential learning is worth using.
Projects and simulations add to cognitive load and direct attention to procedure rather than content.
Drawing on Greg Ashman's book on explicit teaching, she explains why direct instruction works better.

She allows that simulations and well-designed projects can work when students first have knowledge built through explicit instruction, when sensitive topics are handled carefully and teachers are well trained.
She then catalogues simulations that went seriously wrong, including slave auctions and Nazi role-play, and notes that a study of social studies simulations found 12 of 14 had significant problems.

t: Habituate What You Can, Motivate What You Can’t
q: But at the same time, wherever and whenever you can, you want to create the routines and procedures that make motivation unnecessary. Motivation, after all, is about enlisting the will. But routines and procedures? These harness the granite strength of habit.

BUT if those students don’t have anything that they’re used to doing at the start of class, even the most motivated and kind-hearted groups are going to struggle eventually. They’ll get antsy, distracted, jittery.
But here’s the most important thing about routines: since they depend so much on consistency, they’ve got to become habitual for you, too.
In nearly all areas of teaching, perfectionism is uncalled for. But when it comes to reinforcing habit, it really is a good idea to be perfectly consistent.
Thus for both us and for our students, the idea is straightforward: habituate what we can, then motivate what we can't. And throughout it all, simplicity wins the day.
The gist: We want motivation-rich environments all across a student’s school day. The five key beliefs methodology works great for that. But wherever you can, mess around with habit creation, too.
x: Central distinction: motivation 'enlists the will' and requires ongoing effort, while a well-established routine 'harnesses the granite strength of habit' and requires almost none.

Using the start of class as his example, he argues that a class without a consistent opening routine will eventually wear down even the most motivated group and put unsustainable daily pressure on the teacher.
Stuart draws a practical distinction between motivation and habit as classroom-management tools.

A routine only works long-term if the teacher habituates their own follow-through first -- 'it really is a good idea to be perfectly consistent' in running it, even though perfectionism is otherwise unwarranted in teaching.
His conclusion is the title itself: habituate what you can, motivate what you can't, so that motivation is conserved for the harder work (debates, writing, text-based lessons) that habit can't cover.
He notes that routines only work if the teacher, not just the students, is perfectly consistent about running them.

t: How To Build Rapport With A Mask On
q: No longer can you rely on your smile to express warmth, enthusiasm, and pride in your students. A single look that once spoke more than a thousand words has been taken away.
An important key is to first hold their eye contact for a beat. Wait until you’re locked in, then smile and let your creases show.
You’ve heard that 93 percent of communication is nonverbal. If you take away the bottom half of your face, then you absolutely must start using your hands to make up the difference.
Here at SCM, we recommend cutting the amount of talking you normally do by one-third to one-half. You should see dramatic results.
Good teachers, however, find a way. We accept the challenge. We look plainly and honestly at what is in front of us and find a workaround.
But in the long run, when we’re finally beyond masks and social distancing, we’ll all be better communicators, rapport-builders, and teachers.
x: With masks and social distancing removing a teacher's smile and physical closeness, Linsin offers four substitute tools for building rapport.
Strong, held eye contact combined with an exaggerated eye-crinkle is offered as a mask-compatible substitute for a visible smile.
He cites the statistic that most communication is nonverbal to justify leaning harder on gesture and tone once the lower half of the face is hidden.
Cutting overall talking time by roughly a third to a half, while speaking more clearly and pausing more, improves attentiveness.
The four tools are framed as more than sufficient workarounds, since good teachers find a way around any circumstance.

q: It was only after engaging more on Edutwitter that it dawned on me my lessons were task-driven rather than content-driven. Since that realisation, I have been focusing on my explanations, delivery of explanations, and questioning to check for recall and understanding.

In my opinion, a good teaching sequence flows well with each step leading to the next to build a big picture around a central idea. The examples (and non-examples) you use within a teaching sequence are crucial to ensuring your explanation makes sense. Ultimately, the aim of a teaching sequence is to aid our novice learners build their schema so they can make connections between concepts and ideas, and eventually develop expertise.

Once I have identified a teaching sequence (for example surface area to volume ratio in the context of transport in organisms), the next thing I do is to write a list of questions that I want my students to be able to answer by the end. Before I write this list, I do a few things to help me cover all the relevant information required for this teaching sequence.

However, sometimes, even if I have taught a sequence before, I feel there is still scope to improve my explanation. In this case, besides the above sources, I discuss my explanation with someone with more expertise in teaching that sequence. Hearing other ideas and interpretations can be a powerful way to improve one’s own teaching.
I plan what I can say and/or draw to help my students get an answer to each of my core questions. This is a little like a script.
It is important to be aware of potential misconceptions that students may develop. This knowledge of misconceptions could come from experience of teaching and marking assessments on this topic.
x: Castelino's turning point was recognising her lessons were task-driven rather than content-driven and refocusing on clear explanation and questioning.
She defines a good sequence as one in which each step builds toward a central idea using examples and non-examples.
Her core planning step is to write the list of questions students should be able to answer by the end, drawn from specification, textbooks and trusted revision guides.
She treats talking to expert colleagues as a powerful way to improve explanations even for sequences already taught.
Her method is to identify the sequence, write a list of core questions students must answer, and then plan delivery.

She scripts explanations moving from concrete to abstract with planned examples and non-examples, and anticipates misconceptions from experience, examiner reports and an online misconceptions resource.

t: Can We Measure Reading Comprehension Separately From Knowledge?
q: The American education system rests in large part on the assumption that reading comprehension can be tested separately from knowledge. But a recent symposium sponsored by the overseers of the nation’s preeminent reading test revealed how shaky that assumption is.

Lots of evidence shows that it’s impossible to separate reading comprehension from background knowledge, he said. Readers are constantly using their knowledge to fill in gaps in the information provided by the author. In fact, he said, filling in those gaps essentially is reading comprehension.

In providing the definition of a word or phrase, Willingham argued, the test designer is judging which meaning is relevant rather than leaving that to the test-taker—and it’s a judgment that’s central to comprehension. If decisions like that are eliminated from the test, Willingham said, “I think we would be fooling ourselves about how well some kids read.

The most problematic kind of inequity in background knowledge was barely mentioned at the symposium. It’s not between students from different geographic regions or of different genders. It’s between students whose families have different levels of education—and usually, different levels of income.

None of the standard efforts to mitigate the effect of background knowledge has been able to narrow this gap, which has held steady or increased in many other countries as well as the U.S. in recent years. And, it was revealed at the symposium, a trial of the pop-up boxes and other innovative efforts during the 2019 NAEP showed that they were correlated with higher overall scores but led to no difference in the gap between high and low scorers.

Chiasson said that even students who aren’t reading at grade level “have a higher level of comfort” and “feel empowered” when they see test passages with familiar passages and topics. While the data is still preliminary, it indicates that students are more engaged with the new tests and that students of lower socioeconomic status are performing better than they do on traditional tests.

True. But is that possible? Perhaps the NAEP reading framework should be revised to include the idea that it’s testing “a diverse array of content knowledge,” as suggested by board member Martin West, a Harvard education professor. It won’t solve the equity problem, but at least it would provide a more accurate idea of what the problem actually is.
x: She highlights Louisiana's pilot of curriculum-based reading passages as a promising alternative, and suggests NAEP should at least acknowledge it tests a diverse array of content knowledge.

Natalie Wexler reports on a symposium convened by the governing board of the National Assessment of Educational Progress, which is revising its reading framework to compensate for differences in background knowledge.
Willingham's argument is that supplying a definition substitutes the test designer's judgment of meaning for the reader's, so scores overstate how well some children read.
The equity gap that matters most is between families with different education and income levels, which the proposed fixes barely address.

Natalie Wexler reports on a symposium convened by the governing board of the National Assessment of Educational Progress, which is revising its reading framework to compensate for differences in background knowledge.

Because NAEP cannot be curriculum-based, Wexler suggests at least reframing it as testing a diverse array of content knowledge.

t: Self-Disqualification (+ What To Do About It)
q: The older a student gets, the quicker they're likely to disqualify themselves from what you're up to. “Oh, we're doing a math problem? I'm bad at math.” Disqualified.
Self-disqualification is a function of the Belonging belief, which is one of five key beliefs to human motivation. Starting in adolescence, the mind becomes keenly interested in identity-context fit.

When we resolve these questions, the finite resources of the mind, heart, and will are freed up to focus on the work at hand. When we don't, it's like we're running an application in the background of our mind, using up RAM and battery.
Use diverse examples in your instruction. Identity is multifaceted and therefore the way we think about diversity must be, too. But the examples we use do matter — no two have an equal effect.

Make the implicit explicit. For example, teach students how to study effectively — don't just tell them to study. When we assume that all of our students know how to do well what we want them to do well, we make our less confident students more likely to self-disqualify.

Belonging in ourselves? That's another blog post. But as a teaser, it helps to realize that when you're struggling with Belonging you're biased toward interpreting negative events as reflective of your ill fit.
x: He explains the psychological mechanism as a background identity-context-fit question running constantly in the mind ('do people like me do things like this, in places like this?'), which drains mental resources when unresolved.

Stuart's core mechanism: self-disqualification is a Belonging-belief failure where an unresolved 'do I fit here?' question runs in the background of the mind, consuming attention and effort that could go toward the actual task.

q: Many school districts are racing to remove student accountability. Time-out is being outlawed. Suspensions are becoming a no-no.
Remove accountability and bullying , rudeness, disrespect, and every other form of misbehavior will rise like an angry phoenix.
But they won’t tell you what the approach actually is. They won’t say what you are to do as a teacher to protect the rights of your students to learn without interference.
You can’t escape human nature. You can’t escape the fact that when enforcement is removed, the result is more misbehavior.

True accountability, wherein a misbehaving student misses out on something they want to be part of, is good. It teaches critical life lessons like responsibility, empathy, humility, respect, and the desire not to make the same mistake again.
Walk the halls in your fanciest suit, hold your chin up high, and look down your nose at those doing the noble work in the classrooms.
x: The push to remove accountability is attributed to a goal of equal outcomes for every student rather than equal opportunity.
Removing time-out and other traditional accountability is argued to reliably increase bullying, disrespect, and general misbehavior.
The consequences of these policy shifts are said to fall on teachers, parents, and students, not on the leaders promoting them.
Removing time-out and other traditional accountability is argued to reliably increase bullying, disrespect, and general misbehavior.
True accountability — losing access to something valued — is framed as teaching responsibility, empathy, and equal protection under a single standard.
Linsin takes aim at districts replacing traditional accountability — time-out, suspensions, clearly enforced rules — with restorative-style alternatives he considers vague and ineffective.

q: For years, I had been positive that I had failed with Scarlett — positive that, despite my efforts, I hadn't helped her grow as a thinker, speaker, reader, writer, or person.
You know, Mr. Stuart, your class helped me with public speaking. I used to hate it so much, but those pop-up debates showed me that I could do it.
But Scarlett didn't think that. Scarlett had evidence, years later, that the simple work we did in my class contributed at least a percentage point to the improvement of her long-term flourishing.
Tests didn't show it. Grades didn't show it. Her diploma didn't show it. But, nonetheless, there it was that day in the store, standing right in front of me with a big smile.
Here's the point: You and I just don't know the extent of our impact. Doing the right work with the attitude of a craftsperson is too wrought with potential.
For every thank you that you get from a student for the work you've done this year, there are untold dozens that you won't.
x: The anecdote's structural point: Stuart had been 'positive' for years that he'd failed Scarlett, and the disconfirming evidence only surfaced by chance, years later, in a grocery store.
Scarlett tells him, unprompted and beaming, that the pop-up debates from his class helped her land a public-speaking role as a union steward at her job.
The anecdote's structural point: Stuart had been 'positive' for years that he'd failed Scarlett, and the disconfirming evidence only surfaced by chance, years later, in a grocery store.

The encounter becomes the article's thesis: teachers routinely underestimate their own impact because the evidence for it rarely shows up in the places they're trained to look -- tests, grades, diplomas.
His explicit thesis: 'you and I just don't know the extent of our impact,' and the tools schools use to measure success (tests, grades, diplomas) systematically miss this kind of long-tail effect.
Stuart tells the story of running into a former student, Scarlett, at a grocery store years after she was on his roster.
